{"id": "2:282/q47", "question": "Why is error stated before reminding?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:282/q47/p1", "position": "Forgetting is the cause, reminder the intended result", "reasons": "SIBAWAYH (author): Mentioning possible error explains the reason for the reminder, as preparing support for a wall explains the cause without intending it to lean. SIBAWAYH (author): In 2:282, فتذكر is subjunctive because witnessing is commanded so that one woman may remind the other; error is a cause, not the intended aim. IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB (author): أقسط means more just; the record strengthens testimony because it reminds witnesses of all they witnessed. ZAJJAJ (سيبويه والخليل وجميع النحويين الموثوق بعلمهم): The reliable grammarians take أن as purpose: appoint two women so one can remind the other; forgetting is mentioned because it causes the reminder. ZAJJAJ (سيبويه): Sibawayh explains that the cause of reminding is mentioned as its purpose, like preparing a beam to support a wall if it begins to lean. FARISI-HUJJA (author): The testimony is called so one woman may forget and the other remind her; as Sibawayh explains, forgetting is the cause that makes reminding necessary, not the intended outcome. THALABI (author): The author rejects that reading of the rationale because the reminder is conjoined to forgetting, not to male remembrance. WAHIDI-BASIT (author): An is accusative with a purpose sense: call two women as witnesses so that one can remind the other. WAHIDI-BASIT (سيبويه والبصريون): Sibawayh and the Basran grammarians explain that the verse names forgetting because it causes the needed reminder, as preparing a support because a wall may lean. WAHIDI-BASIT (author): Because the clause also says fatudhakkira, the interpretation of an taḍilla as the stated purpose fails: fear of forgetting makes sense, but fear of reminding does not. WAHIDI-BASIT (أبو عمرو بن العلاء): Abū ʿAmr distinguishes the readings: geminated means reminding after forgetting; light means one woman reminds the other because the two together stand in a man’s place. WAHIDI-WAJIZ (author): Writing is fairest before God, makes testimony more reliable because the record reminds witnesses, and best prevents doubt about amount or due date. JISHUMI (سيبويه): Sibawayh explains that straying is stated before reminding because it causes the reminder; the connected actions function as one purpose, as in propping a wall because it is leaning. JISHUMI (author): Jishumi rejects the ‘make her like a man’ gloss because the preceding condition that one may err indicates that reminder means recalling the testimony. BAGHAWI-FULL (author): Writing is most equitable because God commanded it, strengthens testimony by reminding witnesses, and most nearly prevents doubt. KASHSHAF-FULL (author): ‘Lest one err’ means fail to recall the testimony; purpose is phrased by its cause and effect, like preparing a prop for a leaning wall or a weapon for an approaching enemy. KASHSHAF-FULL (author): The cause-effect construction works because the two are closely linked; intent to remind is expressed as intent that one err. IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): The purpose clause does not mean that testimony is taken in order for a woman to err; two women are appointed so one can remind the other if she forgets. BAYDAWI-FULL (author): Witnesses must be people whose uprightness is known; one woman may remind the other if she forgets, with reminder the real rationale and forgetting its trigger. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Pairing Allah with Lord reminds the debtor that God nurtures, repairs, and favors him; Allah comes first because divine authority precedes the reminder of favors. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): With open an, the clause is a purpose-cause: the possibility of forgetting is expressed as the reason for the other to remind, carried by meaning like preparing a prop for a wall that may lean. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): He agrees with al-Zamakhsharī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya: the reading fails linguistically because the verb is not recorded with that causative sense, and logically because both women's testimony, not one woman's reminder, would make the equivalent. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (النحاس عن علي بن سليمان عن أبي العباس): Abū al-ʿAbbās analyzes it as “for fear that one forget”; Abū Jaʿfar rejects this because it would make the purpose that the other woman remind her. SAMIN-DURR (سيبويه): Sibawayh explains that error causes reminder, so cause and result are treated as interchangeable; the purpose is that one woman remind the other, as in preparing a prop for a leaning wall. SAMIN-DURR (أبو جعفر): Abu Ja'far reports that al-Abbas estimated كراهة أن تضل; Abu Ja'far calls it mistaken because it makes the desired reminder something disliked. SAMIN-DURR (author): The repeated إحداهما rather than a pronoun preserves ambiguity because either woman may forget and remind; the generic wording means if one forgets, the other reminds. BURHAN (author): The two women serve to ensure reminder, not to cause error; since forgetting triggers the other’s reminder, the cause is put in place of the intended outcome. BURHAN (سيبويه والبصريون): For this verse, neither “lest one err” nor “for fear of error” makes error a sensible purpose of testimony; the intended purpose is reminder if one forgets, with error as its trigger, like preparing a prop to support a wall if it leans. BIQAI-FULL (author): The future term creates risk of forgetting, which explains the emphasis on writing; hand-to-hand trade is exempt because it is immediately exchanged and unlikely to be disputed. BURSEVI (author): One woman may forget and the other remind her; reminder is the real purpose, while possible error is named as its cause, as in preparing a weapon to repel a possible enemy. eads إن with kasra, puts تضل in the conditional jussive, and raises فتذكر as its response, yielding an independent statement about one witness reminding the other if she forgets. TAB-FULL (الربيع): Al-Rabīʿ explains that one woman may forget and the other reminds her. TAB-FULL (السدي): Al-Suddī says one woman may forget the testimony and the other reminds her. TAB-FULL (الضحاك): Al-Ḍaḥḥāk likewise interprets the clause as one woman forgetting and the other reminding her. ZAJJAJ (بعض أهل اللغة): For the majority’s open أن reading, some grammarians posit a condition moved forward: appoint two women so the remembering one can remind the forgetful one. ZAJJAJ (سيبويه والخليل وجميع النحويين الموثوق بعلمهم): The reliable grammarians take أن as purpose: appoint two women so one can remind the other; forgetting is mentioned because it causes the reminder. IBNABIHATIM (مقاتل بن حيان): The other woman reminds her companion of the testimony. IBNABIHATIM (سعيد بن جبير): The reminding woman is the one who retained her testimony. FARISI-HUJJA (author): The testimony is called so one woman may forget and the other remind her; as Sibawayh explains, forgetting is the cause that makes reminding necessary, not the intended outcome. FARISI-HUJJA (author): The second object of فتذكر إحداهما الأخرى is omitted; the meaning is that one woman reminds the other of the testimony they undertook. FARISI-HUJJA (سفيان بن عيينة): Sufyan ibn Uyayna interprets the phrase as one woman making the other a reminder, but Abu Ali judges this weak because women still need a man for a valid testimony. THALABI (author): The common reading has إن with fatḥa and فتذكر accusative, linked to the preceding clause through an understood causal preposition: one woman may err so the other reminds her. THALABI (author): The author rejects that reading of the rationale because the reminder is conjoined to forgetting, not to male remembrance. WAHIDI-BASIT (أبو عمرو بن العلاء): Abū ʿAmr distinguishes the readings: geminated means reminding after forgetting; light means one woman reminds the other because the two together stand in a man’s place. WAHIDI-BASIT (المفسرون): Exegetes reject the male-equivalence interpretation: women without a man still cannot testify, forgetting should be paired with its opposite, remembering, and equal male status would apply across all legal rulings. WAHIDI-WAJIZ (author): Witnesses are two free adult men of the believers, acceptable for their merit and religion; if one woman forgets, the other reminds her of the testimony. JISHUMI (الربيع والسدي والضحاك وابن زيد): Al-Rabīʿ, al-Suddī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ibn Zayd, and most exegetes take ‘go astray’ as forget, so one woman reminds the other of the testimony. JISHUMI (author): Jishumi rejects the ‘make her like a man’ gloss because the preceding condition that one may err indicates that reminder means recalling the testimony. BAGHAWI-FULL (author): The majority read an tadhilla in the subjunctive, coordinated with fa-tadhakkara, meaning one woman may forget her testimony and the other remind her of the hearing. BAGHAWI-FULL (سفيان بن عيينة): He interprets the wording as making one woman the equivalent of a male witness, but the author prefers the reminder interpretation because it is coordinated with forgetting. IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): The purpose clause does not mean that testimony is taken in order for a woman to err; two women are appointed so one can remind the other if she forgets. Sibawayh compares this construction to preparing a prop for a wall if it leans. TABRISI (author): The particle أن is accusative here, with the sense “because one woman may forget, then the other remind her.” TABRISI (سيبويه): Sībawayh says testimony is requested so one woman may remind the other; possible forgetfulness is the reason for reminding, like shoring a wall because it may lean. RAZI-FULL (سفيان بن عيينة): Sufyan ibn ʿUyayna interprets the second woman as making the first a male-equivalent witness, rather than reminding her of forgotten testimony. QURTUBI-FULL (سفيان بن عيينة وأبو عمرو بن العلاء): Ibn ʿUyayna and Abū ʿAmr understand the lighter reading of the reminder verb as returning a woman's testimony to memory, so two women's testimony totals a man's. QURTUBI-FULL (author): Al-Qurṭubī finds the lighter reminder reading less apt: a reminder naturally answers forgetfulness, and the doubled reading means one woman alerts the other when she forgets. BAYDAWI-FULL (author): Witnesses must be people whose uprightness is known; one woman may remind the other if she forgets, with reminder the real rationale and forgetting its trigger. NASAFI-FULL (author): The two-witness clause explains that one woman may forget the testimony and the other remind her; Ḥamza reads the verb with nominative and gemination under the conditional, while Makki and Baṣri read it accusatively from dhikr. SAMIN-DURR (author): Because أذكرته is causative and takes two objects, the omitted second is testimony: one woman reminds the other of her testimony after forgetting.
